course.title: Habits & Wellbeing
course.description: A practical, evidence-based tour of how habits form and how small changes compound into wellbeing — cue-routine-reward loops, goal-setting, motivation, sleep, and the science of a good life. Built from openly-licensed OER Commons material (CC BY) and peer-reviewed behavioral science. Educational, not therapeutic.

questions.prompt: A habit is best described as a behavior that is…
questions.explanation: Habits are learned behaviors that run automatically once a cue appears — covered in 'How habits work'.

questions.prompt: The three parts of the habit loop are…
questions.explanation: Cue triggers the routine, which delivers a reward that reinforces the loop.

questions.prompt: A well-formed SMART goal is…
options: 'walk 20 minutes after lunch, 5 days a week'
questions.explanation: SMART goals are specific and measurable — see 'Goal-setting'.

questions.prompt: An 'implementation intention' has the form…
options: 'If it is 7am, then I will stretch for five minutes'
questions.explanation: The 'if-then' plan links a situation to an action — a Gollwitzer finding.

questions.prompt: Which statement about motivation is most accurate?
options: Motivation is constant if you care enough
Motivation fluctuates, so systems and cues matter more
questions.explanation: Motivation rises and falls; design beats willpower — see 'Motivation vs discipline'.

questions.prompt: Adults generally function best on how much sleep?
questions.explanation: Most adults need 7–9 hours; chronic short sleep harms focus and mood.

questions.prompt: A simple, well-supported gratitude practice is…
options: listing a few specific good things regularly
questions.explanation: Regular, specific gratitude journaling is linked to higher wellbeing (Emmons & McCullough).

questions.prompt: The fastest way to break a bad habit is usually to…
questions.explanation: Changing the environment and cue is more reliable than willpower — see 'Breaking bad habits'.

lessons.title: How habits work: the cue-routine-reward loop
lessons.grammar_note: Habit loop: cue → routine → reward. Name the parts every time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Break any habit into its cue, routine, and reward, and explain why habits feel automatic. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what triggers a habit in the first place?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *habit* is a behavior your brain has learned to run automatically to save effort. Research on habit formation describes a three-part loop: a *cue* (a trigger — a time, place, feeling, or preceding action), a *routine* (the behavior itself), and a *reward* (the payoff that tells your brain the loop is worth repeating). Over many repetitions the loop moves from deliberate to automatic — a process the brain uses to free up attention. Cravings, an anticipation of the reward, are what pull you through the loop.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: You sit at your desk (cue), open social media (routine), and feel a small hit of novelty and distraction from stress (reward). Notice what the loop actually delivers: often the reward is relief from a feeling, not the app itself. Mapping it — cue: 'I feel restless'; routine: 'scroll'; reward: 'brief escape' — is the first step to redesigning it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Identify the cue, routine, and reward in each: (1) phone buzzes, you check it, you feel connected; (2) you get home tired, you snack, you feel comforted; (3) coffee finishes brewing, you drink it, you feel alert; (4) a meeting ends, you check email, you feel productive. Answers: each is cue → routine → reward. (1) buzz → check → connection; (2) arriving home tired → snack → comfort; (3) brew finishes → drink → alertness; (4) meeting ends → email → sense of productivity.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking habits are about the behavior alone — they are held in place by the reward and triggered by the cue. Mistake: believing habits are permanent (loops can be re-engineered). Exit: (a) Name the three parts of the habit loop. (b) What pulls you through a loop before the reward arrives? Answers: cue, routine, reward; a craving (anticipation of the reward).

lessons.title: Building good habits and breaking bad ones
lessons.grammar_note: To build: make the cue obvious and the reward satisfying. To break: hide the cue and change the reward.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use two proven levers — cue design and habit stacking — to build a habit, and disrupt an unwanted one by changing its cue. Warm-up: from the last lesson, which part of the loop is easiest to control in your environment?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Because habits are cue-driven, the most reliable lever is your *environment*, not your willpower. To build a habit: make the cue obvious (leave running shoes by the door), make the routine easy (start absurdly small — two minutes), and make the reward immediate and satisfying. *Habit stacking* attaches a new habit to an existing one: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will write one sentence in my journal.' To break a habit: make the cue invisible (remove the trigger) and keep the same reward through a healthier routine. Studies of behavior change find that people who alter their surroundings succeed more than those who rely on motivation alone.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Redesign a bad habit's cue and reward. Bad loop — cue: phone on the nightstand; routine: scroll in bed; reward: distraction from a busy mind. Redesign: move the charger across the room (cue removed) and keep the reward by swapping the routine — a two-page paperback on the pillow now delivers the same wind-down. Same reward, new routine, disabled cue.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Design a fix for each. (1) You want to floss but forget — add a cue. (2) You snack on chips while watching TV — disrupt the cue. (3) You want to read more but never start — shrink the routine. (4) You check email first thing and lose your morning — change the environment. (5) You want a daily walk — stack it. Sample answers: (1) stack it: 'After I brush, I floss.' (2) Keep chips out of the room; put fruit in view. (3) Commit to one page, not one chapter. (4) Leave the phone in another room overnight; open a planner first. (5) 'After lunch, I put on shoes and walk to the corner.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: relying on willpower instead of redesigning the environment. Mistake: starting too big — a habit you skip on a hard day isn't sticky yet. Exit: (a) To break a habit, what do you do to its cue? (b) What does habit stacking attach a new habit to? Answers: make the cue invisible / remove it; an existing habit you already do.

lessons.title: Goal-setting: SMART goals and implementation intentions
lessons.grammar_note: Goals set the target; implementation intentions ('if-then') set the trigger.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Turn a vague wish into a SMART goal and pair it with an if-then plan that fires automatically. Warm-up: why might 'get fit' fail where 'walk after lunch' succeeds?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A vague goal gives your brain nothing to act on. A *SMART* goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound: 'walk 20 minutes after lunch, five days a week, for the next month.' But a goal names the destination, not the trigger. *Implementation intentions* — studied by Peter Gollwitzer — supply the trigger with an if-then plan: 'If it is 12:30 and I've finished lunch, then I put on my shoes and walk.' Across many studies, people who write if-then plans act on their goals substantially more often, because the situation itself cues the behavior — the same mechanism that makes habits automatic.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Wish: 'I should study Spanish more.' SMART version: 'Study Spanish for 15 minutes, Monday to Friday, for three weeks.' Implementation intention: 'If it is 8pm and I've cleared the dinner table, then I open the app and do one lesson.' Notice the if-then reuses the habit loop: a concrete cue (8pm, table cleared) triggers the routine. You can also plan for obstacles: 'If I'm too tired, then I do just one flashcard.'

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Rewrite each wish as a SMART goal plus an if-then plan. (1) 'Drink more water.' (2) 'Exercise regularly.' (3) 'Read more books.' (4) 'Save money.' Sample answers: (1) 'Drink 6 glasses of water daily this month' + 'If I sit down at my desk, then I fill my water bottle.' (2) 'Strength-train 3x/week for a month' + 'If it's Mon/Wed/Fri morning, then I do a 15-minute routine before breakfast.' (3) 'Read 10 pages a night for two weeks' + 'If I get into bed, then I read before touching my phone.' (4) 'Move $50 to savings each payday for 3 months' + 'If my paycheck lands, then I transfer $50 first.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: setting outcome-only goals ('lose 10 pounds') with no plan for the daily action that gets you there. Mistake: making goals so ambitious they're unachievable, which kills momentum. Exit: (a) What does the 'M' in SMART stand for? (b) What is the structure of an implementation intention? Answers: Measurable; 'If [situation], then [action].'

questions.prompt: The reward in a habit loop mainly serves to…
options: reinforce the loop so it repeats
questions.explanation: The reward tells the brain the loop is worth repeating.

questions.prompt: The most reliable lever for changing habits is usually…
questions.explanation: Changing surroundings beats relying on willpower.

questions.prompt: Habit stacking works by attaching a new habit to…
questions.explanation: 'After [current habit], I will [new habit].'

questions.prompt: Which is a properly formed SMART goal?
questions.explanation: Specific, measurable, and time-bound.

questions.prompt: An implementation intention is written as…
questions.explanation: The if-then plan links a cue to an action.

questions.prompt: To break an unwanted habit, the first move is usually to…
questions.explanation: Disrupt the trigger that starts the loop.

lessons.title: Motivation vs discipline — and the energy behind both
lessons.grammar_note: Motivation starts a habit; systems sustain it. Sleep, stress, and focus are the fuel.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why systems outperform willpower, and name the basics — sleep, stress management, focus — that keep behavior change possible. Warm-up: think of a habit you kept even when you didn't feel like it. What carried it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Motivation* is the feeling that makes you want to act; it naturally rises and falls. *Discipline* or self-control helps, but research suggests willpower is easier when you don't have to use much of it — people who report high self-control often just have better *systems* and environments, so temptation shows up less. That's why cues, if-then plans, and habit stacking matter more than trying to want it harder. Underneath all of this is your *capacity*: chronic short sleep (most adults need 7–9 hours) erodes focus, mood, and self-control; unmanaged *stress* narrows attention and pushes you toward old routines; and *focus* is protected by removing distractions, not by trying to concentrate through them. Behavior change is far easier when you're rested and your environment is calm.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Redesign for low-motivation days. Instead of 'I'll exercise when I feel like it' (motivation-dependent), build a floor: 'If it's a workout day, then I put on shoes and do the two-minute version.' On tired days the two-minute floor still fires; on good days you do more. You've replaced fragile motivation with a system — and by protecting sleep the night before, you make the good days more common.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each, name whether it's leaning on motivation or on a system, then improve it. (1) 'I'll start when I'm inspired.' (2) 'Phone charges in the kitchen so I sleep better.' (3) 'I'll just power through the distractions.' (4) 'I meditate after I brush my teeth.' Answers: (1) motivation → add an if-then floor; (2) system (good); (3) willpower → remove the distraction (close tabs, silence phone); (4) system (habit-stacked, good).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a lapse as proof you 'lack discipline' — usually the system or your energy failed, not your character. Mistake: ignoring sleep and stress while trying to build hard new habits. Exit: (a) Why do high-self-control people often struggle less? (b) Name one 'capacity' basic that protects self-control. Answers: better systems mean they face temptation less often; sleep (or stress management / focus).

lessons.title: Positive psychology: gratitude and meaning
lessons.grammar_note: Wellbeing is more than the absence of stress — it's built with practices, like habits.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe what positive psychology studies and practice two evidence-based habits — gratitude and connecting to meaning. Warm-up: name one small thing that reliably lifts your mood.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Positive psychology* is the scientific study of what helps people flourish, not just the treatment of what goes wrong. One influential model, Seligman's *PERMA*, describes five buildable ingredients of wellbeing: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment. Two of its most-studied practices are habit-shaped. *Gratitude*: in studies by Emmons and McCullough, people who regularly wrote down a few specific things they were grateful for reported higher wellbeing than those who listed hassles. *Meaning*: connecting daily actions to something you value — a person, a purpose, a contribution — sustains effort and buffers stress. Note the framing: these are educational practices for everyday wellbeing, not treatments for clinical conditions, which call for a qualified professional.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Turn gratitude into a habit loop. Cue: 'After I get into bed' (an existing anchor). Routine: 'write three specific good things from today' — specific beats generic ('my friend called to check in,' not 'friends'). Reward: a calmer, more positive wind-down. For meaning, add a why: 'I'm learning this so I can help my family,' which links a routine to a value and makes it more durable.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Rewrite this vague entry to be specific: 'I'm grateful for my life.' (2) Habit-stack a gratitude practice onto a morning routine. (3) Which PERMA element does 'called a friend today' most support? (4) Add a meaning-based 'why' to the goal 'exercise more.' Sample answers: (1) 'I'm grateful my neighbor helped carry groceries today.' (2) 'After I pour my coffee, I name one thing I'm looking forward to.' (3) Relationships (and Positive emotion). (4) 'I exercise so I have energy to play with my kids.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating positive psychology as forced positivity or ignoring real problems — it complements, not replaces, dealing with difficulties. Mistake: keeping gratitude vague, which weakens the effect. Exit: (a) What does the 'M' in PERMA stand for? (b) Why does specificity matter in a gratitude practice? Answers: Meaning; specific items feel genuine and have a stronger link to wellbeing than generic ones.

questions.prompt: Compared with willpower, systems and cues are…
questions.explanation: Design and environment beat relying on motivation.

questions.prompt: Chronic short sleep tends to…
questions.explanation: Most adults need 7–9 hours; short sleep undermines change.

questions.prompt: In PERMA, the 'R' stands for…
questions.explanation: Relationships are a core ingredient of wellbeing.

questions.prompt: An effective gratitude practice is…
questions.explanation: Specific, regular entries are linked to higher wellbeing.

questions.prompt: The best response to a habit lapse is usually to…
options: check what system or energy failed and adjust
questions.explanation: Lapses point to a design or capacity gap, not a character flaw.

questions.prompt: Linking a routine to a personal 'why' mainly helps by…
options: making effort more durable through meaning
questions.explanation: Meaning sustains effort and buffers stress.

lessons.title: Applied project: design a 30-day habit plan

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Design a realistic 30-day plan to build one habit that supports a real goal of yours (for example: move daily, sleep earlier, read, or a gratitude practice). You won't be graded on the outcome — you'll be graded on how well your plan uses the science from this course. Keep it educational and practical; this is a self-improvement plan, not a treatment for any health condition.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State your goal as a SMART goal (specific, measurable, time-bound). 2) Map the habit loop you'll build: name the cue, the routine (start with a two-minute version), and the reward. 3) Write an implementation intention: 'If [situation], then [action].' 4) Habit-stack it onto something you already do daily. 5) Design your environment: one thing you'll add to make the cue obvious, and one distraction you'll remove. 6) Plan for obstacles with a backup if-then for low-energy days, and note one 'capacity' basic (sleep, stress, or focus) you'll protect. 7) Choose how you'll track it (a simple checkmark calendar works).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Goal is SMART, not vague. ✔ You named all three parts of the habit loop, and the routine starts small. ✔ You wrote a clear if-then implementation intention. ✔ The habit is stacked onto an existing anchor. ✔ You changed the environment (added a cue, removed a distraction). ✔ You have a backup plan and protect one capacity basic. If all six are true, your plan is built on real behavioral science — now run it for 30 days and adjust from what you observe.
